title: Three-Property Rule Strategy
name: Three-Property Rule Strategy
metaTitle: Three-Property Rule Strategy for Dallas 1031 Exchanges
metaDescription: Using the three-property identification rule on a Dallas exchange: building a real backup list without leaning on the 200 percent alternative.

sections.html: Most Dallas exchanges run under the three-property rule without anyone needing to think much about the alternatives, simply because naming up to three candidates, regardless of their combined value, covers almost every situation. The strategy question isn't whether the rule applies, it's whether the three names on your letter are actually three real options or one strong deal and two placeholders.

sections.heading: What the Three-Property Rule Actually Allows
sections.html:
An investor can identify up to three properties as of the 45th day, with no limit on their combined fair market value, and go on to close any one, two, or all three within the 180-day exchange period. This is different from the 200 percent rule, which allows more than three properties but caps their combined value, and it's the rule most Dallas investors default to because three real candidates is usually enough given the depth of local inventory.

The value flexibility matters more than people initially realize. An investor exchanging out of a modest relinquished property can still identify a single large replacement worth far more than the sale proceeds, as long as they can actually finance and close on it inside the window.

sections.heading: Why Three Placeholder Names Rarely Amounts to a Real Strategy
sections.html:
We see identification letters built under pressure that list one property the investor actually wants and two others added just to satisfy the rule's requirement of naming something. That approach only works if the primary deal actually closes, and it leaves an investor with no real fallback if financing falls through or diligence surfaces a problem in the final weeks before day 180.

A Dallas seller on the primary candidate will sense the difference too. A buyer whose backup properties are clearly placeholders often negotiates from a weaker position than one who's genuinely prepared to walk toward a real alternative.

sections.heading: Building a List of Three Genuine Candidates
sections.html:
We treat all three slots as live options from the start, which means underwriting the backups just as closely as the favorite, so that any of the three could actually close if needed. In a market like Dallas with meaningful depth across net-lease, multifamily, and industrial stock, this is usually achievable inside the 45-day window if sourcing starts the day the relinquished sale goes under contract.

That depth is exactly why the three-property rule fits this metro so well. An investor exchanging out of a Dallas property rarely has to compromise on asset class just to fill out a genuine three-candidate list.

sections.heading: When a Different Rule Might Fit Better
sections.html:
The three-property rule stops making sense when an investor genuinely wants exposure to more than three assets, such as splitting exchange proceeds across several smaller net-lease properties instead of one larger building. In that case the 200 percent rule, which caps combined identified value at twice the relinquished property's sale price, may be the better fit, though that's a separate strategy with its own tradeoffs.

We raise this question early with every Dallas client, since deciding between the two approaches after a candidate list is already forming is far harder than deciding before the search even begins.

sections.heading: What Goes Into a Genuine Three-Property List
sections.html:
Before we help finalize a three-property identification letter, each candidate gets a full review rather than a passing glance:

  • Independent underwriting on financing, lease terms, and title
  • Confirmation the seller is realistically willing to hold the deal open through a Dallas closing timeline
  • A clear sense of which candidate is the primary target versus genuine backups
  • Alignment with the investor's actual hold strategy rather than only proximity to the relinquished property's value
  • A realistic read on how long each seller will wait before moving to a backup buyer of their own

faqs.q: Does the three-property rule limit how much the identified properties are worth combined?
faqs.a: No. Under the three-property rule, you can identify up to three properties of any combined fair market value, which is different from the 200 percent rule that caps total identified value but allows more than three properties.

faqs.q: Is it a problem to list backup properties I don't actually want to buy?
faqs.a: It can be, if those backups aren't real options. A list with two placeholder names only works if your primary deal closes without any issue, and it leaves you exposed if that deal falls through late in the 180-day window.

faqs.q: How many properties should actually be underwritten before finalizing a three-property list?
faqs.a: All three, ideally, rather than only whichever one looks strongest at first glance. Treating every slot as a genuine candidate rather than a formality means you have real, workable options if financing or diligence issues surface on your top choice.

faqs.q: When would the 200 percent rule make more sense than the three-property rule for a Dallas investor?
faqs.a: When you genuinely want to spread exchange proceeds across more than three properties, such as several smaller net-lease assets instead of one larger building. That's a different strategy with its own value-cap tradeoffs, and it's worth discussing early rather than after a list is already underway.

faqs.q: Can I close on more than one of my three identified properties?
faqs.a: Yes. You can close on any one, two, or all three properties named on a valid three-property identification letter, as long as each closing happens within the 180-day exchange period, and each acquisition is otherwise structured correctly as part of the same exchange.
